stories.headline: Music for nothing and clicks for free: The bane of streaming platforms in India
stories.title: Music for nothing and clicks for free: The bane of streaming platforms in India
stories.summary: Eighteen-year-old Archit Menon, a college student in Kochi, logs in to two apps the most every day. The first is Instagram, where he scrolls through Reels between classes, half-watching, half-listening; the second is Spotify, where eventually he might find the full version of a song he caught a whiff of on Reels and liked. Most songs on his playlist have been added in this manner.For years he paid nothing for either feed, putting up with the intermittent ads on Spotify, until his consumption increased drastically. “At first I was fine with ads once every 30 minutes. But as I got hooked to my favourite artistes and podcasts, ads started bothering me,” he says. What finally pushed him to pay up was not a discount or a marketing nudge, but the fact that he now wanted to access his playlists while offline, better sound quality that did justice to his Bose headphones, and not letting his music queue be interrupted. “I’m not paying for the songs only but also the seamlessness,” he says.When services like Saavn (later JioSaavn) and Gaana launched in India in 2007 and 2010 respectively, the country’s smartphone and internet industries were nascent, and music platforms were primarily internet-based. Global music streaming platforms entered the Indian market in 2018-2019, with the launch of Amazon Music and Spotify AB. Yatish Mehrishi, CEO, ENIL, under which Gaana operates. photo by Swapnil Sakhare for Forbes IndiaWhen the global players launched their services in countries like the US and Europe, they had paid subscriptions as their core offering, with free listening used to nudge users to upgrade. But when these platforms came to India, they focussed on building a large listenership, and did this through free music. The battle was about getting the largest slice of India’s massive population pie. But now that the same population has gotten hooked to free content and occasional ads—much like All India Radio and FM radio that preceded streaming—getting this listenership to pay is turning out to be a price war.What is queering the pitch further is the fact that listeners are discovering and engaging with music in a fragmented manner across social media platforms such as Instagram, YouTube Shorts, concerts and creator platforms. Thus, no single platform can control the listener’s full journey anymore.The paywall playbook“People often get misled by India’s population of 1.5 billion,” says Yatish Mehrishi, CEO of Entertainment Network India Limited (ENIL) under which Gaana operates. “The assumption was that if you built a habit, everyone would eventually pay. But India is extremely diverse, with significant income disparity. It’s unrealistic to expect the entire population to become paying subscribers.” For years, he says, platforms chased downloads and habit formation, while content costs kept climbing as record labels demanded higher licensing fees, costs that advertising alone could not offset.However, that is starting to change, gradually. According to the FICCI-EY Media & Entertainment Report 2026, India’s paid music subscriptions grew 37 percent in a single year to reach 14.4 million, crossing ₹1,000 crore in audio subscription revenue for the first time. “Paid subscriptions [across platforms] have grown from roughly 7 million to around 15 million over a short period. While those numbers are still modest compared to global markets, they show that consumers are beginning to see value in paying for music,” says Mehrishi. “Indians have paid for music, whether it was LPs, cassettes, CDs or even pirated cassettes. The issue isn’t the ability to pay; it’s the willingness to pay.”Ashish Pherwani, partner for media and entertainment at EY, agrees. “India’s music industry has been providing music for free, or ad-supported, since it got digitised. Indians lost the habit of paying for music over time,” he says. “Global and Indian platforms have now started correcting this anomaly by restricting features to free users, which has helped the paid subscription base to reach about 15 million. We expect that to double in the next three years.” Streaming features such as rewind, offline downloads, unlimited skips and on-demand song selection, once freely available, now need to be paid for. Media reports indicate that platforms, music labels and independent consultants expect the number of paid subscribers to rise to 50-75 million in the next decade.When Amazon Music entered the Indian market, it was with an Amazon Prime-bundled, ad-supported version. “We did not see significant demand for paid premium audio. At the time, the market was dominated by free and telco-bundled offerings, with little differentiation between paid and free services,” says Rishi Mirchandani, vice president of licensing and strategy at Amazon Music.The company launched Amazon Music Unlimited this June, at ₹99 a month for Prime members and ₹119 for others, alongside a new ad-supported Amazon Music Free tier. “Now we’re seeing a shift in India too,” Mirchandani says. “Customers are showing a greater willingness to pay for premium audio experiences.”Rishabh Gupta, head of Amazon Music India, says, “India’s addressable audience for pure-play audio streaming is still expanding. We have a large and growing middle class, and a huge segment of listeners haven’t moved onto pure-play audio streaming. So, for us, acquisition isn’t a phase that’s behind us; it’s ongoing.”Also Read: How India's music makers are charting their own successHowever, he believes, acquisition alone is no longer enough. “Alongside, there’s an equal opportunity to deepen engagement through experiences that reflect how people actually listen,” he says. Amazon Music’s three-tier structure—Prime, Unlimited and Free—is the platform’s attempt to serve every kind of listener. “That’s the real shift for us, from serving one audience to serving all of them.”Amazon’s tiered approach is not unique and is now the industry’s default model. Mehrishi of Gaana predicts India’s audio market will eventually resemble the segmentation seen in video streaming. “Like Netflix or Amazon Prime Video, the market will evolve into multiple segments. Some consumers will subscribe, while others will remain on hybrid or ad-supported models,” he says. Music streaming, he adds, hasn’t seen the rapid subscription growth video experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, so segmentation will matter more as paid adoption climbs toward 25-30 million users.As of December 2025, India had about 14 million paid music subscriptions, compared to more than 200 million paid video subscriptions, according to a 2026 report by EY and the Indian Music Industry (IMI), titled ‘How India Listens, Streams and Pays for Music’.One of the significant differences between the audio and video streaming industries is that while video streaming platforms have unique content libraries, films or series, the availability of which they shuffle, audio streaming platforms all have the same content libraries, which are available all the time. There is almost nothing that differentiates one platform from another where content is concerned, and their individual unique selling points (USPs) lie in features such as seamless shareability on social media platforms, which can help users discover new music. The unique content of video platforms means a single user may want to subscribe to multiple platforms, while that incentive is not there for users of audio platforms.Andrew Smith, head of digital strategy at Virtuoso Music, which launched in India this June, cites paid listening growth of “more than a third last year” as evidence India is “crossing the line that other markets crossed before it. Every market that closed its free-to-paid gap saw growth take off on the other side,” he says. “It would be no great stretch to suggest India could reach over 140 million paid subscriptions within a decade.”The UK-headquartered company’s India entry marked its first move into South Asia, with a multilingual slate across Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil and Telugu. Virtuoso Music’s head of new business and music, Sahaj Miya, adds, “Paid subscriptions are at the start of their steepest climb, and the next decade of growth for the platforms will be exponential, bringing India much closer to the global operating model.”Not everyone believes progress will be smooth. Pherwani of EY says, “In the long run, the business model that will work will be driven by fans who pay for subscriptions, merchandise and concerts. Advertising and ad-funded content remain adjunct to the main revenue sources for streamers.” This is a reminder that subscriptions, however fast they grow, may never be the whole story. Rishabh Gupta, head, Amazon Music India. Photo by Swapnil Sakhare for Forbes IndiaVolume vs valueThe uncomfortable reality at the centre of India’s streaming story, according to many, is that the country is huge by volume and unremarkable by value. “India records around 5 billion audio and video streams a year, making it one of the largest markets globally by volume. But by value, we are still around the 15th to 20th largest market,” Mehrishi says.That gap, he adds, is not a mystery. The size of India’s population, the large number of films being produced, and linguistic diversity makes monetisation difficult. “Ten years ago, India and China were comparable music markets. Today, China is among the world’s largest by value, while India still ranks around 15th.” According to IFPI’s Global Music Report 2026, globally, recorded music revenue from streaming platforms reached $29.6 billion in 2025, with paid subscriptions rising by 85 million to 837 million. However, India’s contributions in value terms are modest and it ranks 15 in the world where paying listeners are concerned.What India does have, unusually, is an overwhelming preference for its own music, which takes time to find its way onto the platforms, if at all. Domestic collection accounts for roughly 89 percent—among the highest in the world—of all music streaming in the country, according to IFPI data, which is one of the highest home-market shares anywhere in the world. This is one of the reasons global streaming platforms have had to invest heavily in regional catalogues and local artiste partnerships rather than relying solely on international hits. Countries like Japan, South Korea, China and Brazil also prefer their own music compared to international genres.Rajesh Sethi, partner and sector leader for media, entertainment and sports at PwC India, says, “India’s music streaming industry is thriving, powered by smartphone penetration, cheap data, and rising demand for regional content. However, monetisation lags due to price sensitivity and preference for free, ad-supported services. The good news, however, is that consumers are increasingly willing to pay, digital payments are improving, and advertisers are investing in audio too.”In India, the popularity of regional and domestic film and non-film music is an added parameter for platforms to navigate. The share of film music among Indian listeners fell from 65 percent in 2023 to 57 percent in 2025, according to the FICCI-EY report, as independent and regional music took centrestage.Spotify India has watched this play out. “When Spotify launched in India seven years ago, over 70 percent of consumption was international music. Today, that has inverted, with over 70 percent of our consumption being of local content,” says Dhruvank Vaidya, head of music and podcasts. The platform’s artiste-first bets—programmes like RADAR, Rap 91 and I-Pop—were built on the belief that Indian listeners wanted to go beyond film soundtracks if given the option. About half of Spotify India’s annual Top 50 songs are non-film. For instance, Haryanvi music streams have grown nearly sevenfold between 2023 and 2026, spreading well beyond the NCR into cities like Jaipur, Bhopal, Lucknow and Bengaluru.Gupta sees a similar pattern among Amazon Music’s listeners. “The majority of consumption still comes from soundtracks of films or any other videos in India. And the single largest language is still Hindi,” he says; about 83 percent of listeners seek out Hindi music, followed by English and Punjabi, with Tamil and Telugu growing fast; regional breakouts witness spikes in listenership rather than form trends. “We’ll see one-offs: For example, in the last few months, Marathi has been doing really well because of ‘Shaky’ and ‘Gulabi Sadi’. You need a more sustained supply of content in every language and genre. We see those trends across the board, but they’re still sporadic,” says Gupta.Publishing revenue, too, is finding its wings, with creator royalty collections growing more than 40 percent in 2024, among the fastest rates globally, and digital platforms contributing over 80 percent of collections, according to the CISAC Global Collections Report 2025. But ownership and artiste rights remain an issue. Taking advantage of this, Virtuoso’s Miya says the firm is betting on Indian catalogue and artiste ownership because no other platform is focussing on artiste benefits. “The next chapter of the global music story will be written in India,” he says. “We are here to invest in it, bringing our creator-first model built on artist equity.” Unlike the traditional buyout model, with Virtuoso’s revenue model, artistes keep a stake in their music and continue to earn as it generates revenue from streaming and other commercial uses worldwide.Smith adds that India is part of a broader emerging-market pattern: “We have seen it play out globally, with Brazil and Latin America making that shift and compounding ever since. India is crossing that line now, at far greater scale.”Beyond playlistsBesides monetisation, the fragmentation of music consumption is the terrain these platforms have to fight on.A decade ago, Mehrishi says, “Music discovery happened largely through radio. Then YouTube became the primary discovery platform. Today, discovery increasingly happens through Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts.” He is not alarmed by this. “I see this as beneficial for streaming services because music is integral to short-form video. Without music, a Reel is flat. People discover songs through these platforms, and if they like a track, they eventually come to a streaming service to hear the full version.”Sethi adds that these visual, bite-sized formats “speed up discovery-to-listening cycles and boost viral sharing and repeat plays.”Some see the response to fragmentation as not a rewritten business model but as a redefined role. “It’s less about rethinking the business model and more about rethinking what role we want to serve in a listener’s everyday life,” Gupta says. Amazon Music’s answer has been to add exclusive content and experiences in addition to catalogue access. “Because fans want to feel close to the artiste, not just stream them,” Gupta says, pointing to partnering with music releases of films Param Sundari (2025) and Dhurandhar (2026). Devices, too, are part of the strategy: There is a ₹59-a-month Amazon Music Unlimited plan built for Alexa-enabled devices.In the coming years, as Pherwani says, live music and fandom indicate where the industry’s energy and revenue are heading. Mehrishi points to merchandising as an early-stage but inevitable growth line. “Younger audiences have a much stronger sense of fandom than previous generations. They’re willing to spend money on concerts, merchandise and experiences around their favourite artistes.”Vaidya calls it a structural convergence. “Live touring, brand partnerships, sync opportunities—things that were once almost exclusively tied to film music—are now opening up for independent artistes. The boundary between film and non-film has already started to dissolve.”For a market this large and this young, the listening will keep growing; the challenge is to make them pay.

stories.headline: Military modernisation driven by self-reliant and future-ready defence sector is govt’s top priority: Rajnath Singh
stories.title: Military modernisation driven by self-reliant and future-ready defence sector is govt’s top priority: Rajnath Singh
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 14: “The Government, under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, is according the highest priority to the modernisation of the defence forces driven by a self-reliant and future-ready defence sector,” said Defence Minister Rajnath Singh in his address to the soldiers through Akashvani on the eve of 80th Independence Day on August 14, 2026. Highlighting the transformative shift witnessed by the defence sector in the last 12 years due to the initiatives such as ‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’ and ‘Make-in-India’, Raksha Mantri asserted that India has become a nation which is effectively catering to its own security needs, while emerging as a global defence manufacturing hub and a net defence exporter. Singh emphasised that the domestic defence production, which stood at just Rs 46,000 crore in 2014, has skyrocketed to a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in the Financial Year (FY) 2025-26, nearly a four-fold increase over the last decade. This achievement, he said, is a testament to the structural changes that have taken place in the defence sector. He pointed out that Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs) and other public sector entities accounted for approximately 76% of the total defence production, with the private sector contributing 24%, up from 22% in the previous fiscal year. This growing participation of the private sector signals a continuously improving business environment within the defence sector, he said. Defence Minister added that defence exports, which stood at a mere Rs 686 crore in FY 2013-14, surged to an all-time high of Rs 38,424 crore in FY 2025-26, an increase of over 5,500%. He described the feat as the most compelling evidence of Aatmanirbharta in the defence sector. “Today, India has 145 defence exporters, and our products are being exported to over 80 countries. I am confident that we will achieve our defence exports target of Rs 50,000 crore by 2029,” he said. He also pointed out that the defence budget has risen from Rs 2.53 lakh crore in FY 2013-14 to Rs 7.85 lakh crore in FY 2026-27, which is a reflection of India's growing commitment to future defence technologies. “Capital expenditure has grown from Rs 94,588 crore to Rs 2.19 lakh crore. Our focus on Research & Development has also intensified. The R&D budget, which stood at Rs 15,283 crore in FY 2014-15, has increased by 90% to Rs 29,100 crore in FY 2026-27,” he said. Defence Minister added that over the past year, the Defence Acquisition Council has granted Acceptance of Necessity for projects worth over Rs 8.75 lakh crore, which highlights the Government’s emphasis on defence modernisation. He listed the fundamental reforms undertaken in defence procurement to accelerate this modernisation process, including a two-fold increase in financial ceiling for Field Commanders to strengthen operational efficiency, and facilitation of procurement worth more than Rs 1.25 lakh crore through the revenue route to boost indigenisation. Singh acknowledged the enthusiastic participation of the defence forces in the journey towards Aatmanirbharta. He stressed that India’s defence self-reliance drive is gaining momentum as indigenous warships, aircraft and advanced military systems are strengthening the capabilities of the Defence Forces. He asserted that DRDO and the defence forces are positioning India at the forefront of technologies for future warfare amidst the evolving defence landscape. He made special mention of the successful test of the first Tactical Advanced Range Augmentation system, which has the capability to transform conventional weapons into precision-guided munitions. “The testing of the Advanced Agni Missile, equipped with MIRV technology, has added a new dimension to the strategic deterrence capabilities. Successful trials of the Long-Range Land Attack Cruise Missile, RudraM-II Air-to-Surface Missile, Naval Anti-Ship Missile-SR, and Pinaka Long-Range Guided Rocket have provided unprecedented strength to the nation’s strike capabilities,” he added. On the successful test of Active Cooled Full-Scale Scramjet Combustor for over 1,200 seconds, Rajnath Singh stated that the feat has placed India among the select group of nations capable of developing hypersonic missile technology. He added that the nation’s air defence capabilities have been further bolstered by the first successful test of the indigenous Kusha’ Long-Range Surface-to-Air Missile. Defence Minister underlined that border area development is a focus area of the Government as the objective is to enhance defence preparedness and connectivity with border areas. He lauded the defence forces for being the ‘first responders’ to carry out relief and rescue operations whenever an unfortunate natural disaster occurs in the country or abroad. Singh reiterated the Government’s commitment towards the welfare of serving and retired defence forces personnel as well as their families, describing them as a reflection of honor, dignity, and self-respect. “Over the past five years, there has been a 300% increase in the budget of the Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme. Furthermore, under the Armed Forces Flag Day Fund, the Penury Grant has been doubled from Rs 4,000 to Rs 8,000, the Education Grant from Rs 1,000 to Rs 2,000 and the Marriage Grant from Rs 50,000 to Rs 1,00,000. Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, heading a three-judge Bench, said highways act as a lifeline for ordinary people.

The court was hearing a petition filed by the Kuki Women Organisation for Human Rights seeking the removal of the blockade on National Highway 2 and restoration of supply of essential services to the State.
“Why can’t both groups realise something?

stories.title: Govt taking comprehensive reforms to curb exam paper leaks, protect future of youths: President Murmu
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 14: Underlining that students are the "architects of India's future," President Droupadi Murmu on Friday said the government is taking comprehensive steps to reform public examinations to completely curb paper leaks and unfair means, making the system transparent, secure, and trustworthy. In her address to the nation on the eve of the country's 80th Independence Day, the president stressed that just as government and society remain united to ensure national security, everyone must contribute through joint and concerted efforts to safeguard the present and future of students. "Public examinations become gateways to opportunities for our students. The government is undertaking comprehensive steps to reform these examinations. The objectives of these reforms are to completely curb the use of unfair means in public examinations, make the examination system more transparent, more secure, and more trustworthy for the youth," she said. Her remarks assume significance in the backdrop of recent nationwide Gen Z and student-led protests demanding systemic overhauls, fast-track investigations, and stringent legal action following high-profile paper leak irregularities in competitive examinations. Highlighting the spirit of enterprise among young citizens, she said youths are increasingly embracing a culture of job creation rather than job seeking. "Many of our youth are embracing the culture of job creation as they pursue the path of self-employment. The participation of young entrepreneurs has led to the creation of a strong start-up ecosystem in our country. Major global enterprises are impressed by the talent and dedication of Indian youth and entrust them with leadership roles," she added. The president said such achievers have enhanced the reputation of India's youth power globally and reaffirmed her faith in the country's bright future. Turning to holistic development, the president said that the physical and mental well-being of the youth forms the cornerstone of the nation's future, adding that families and society share the collective responsibility to motivate them. She highlighted sports as a key vehicle for youth development and nation-building under the flagship 'Khelo India' programme. "Under the Khelo India programme, a sports ecosystem is being developed across the country, from the grassroots to the national level. The government is making unprecedented investments to promote sports, yielding remarkable leaps in the achievements of our sportspersons in international tournaments," she said. President Murmu also lauded the "unmatched valour" of the Indian Armed Forces, saying Operation Sindoor demonstrated the country's capability to execute precision counter-terror operations and sent a firm message that terror elements and their backers will face consequences regardless of where they hide. She recalled the anniversary of the military action alongside historic observances like Kargil Vijay Diwas, reaffirming India's tradition of overcoming forces hostile to humanity. "On the 26th of July, we observed Kargil Vijay Diwas. Earlier, on the 7th of May, we commemorated the completion of one year since the launch of Operation Sindoor. We remembered the unmatched valour of our Armed Forces. That historic operation against terrorism demonstrated the capability of the Indian Armed Forces to act with precision," she said. She said the operation delivered an unequivocal warning to enemies. "It sent a clear and firm message to terrorists and those who support them, that no matter where they hide, they will have to face the consequences of their actions." The President also highlighted the strategic measures accompanying the counter-terror posture, describing the decision to suspend the Indus Waters Treaty with the nation harbouring terror networks as a "decisive step in the interest of our nation, especially the farmers." On internal security, she termed the eradication of Naxalism a monumental achievement for the country after decades of struggle. "For decades, Naxalism posed a serious challenge to the nation. Making India Naxal free is a major achievement. Today, enthusiasm prevails in the areas once affected by Naxalism," she said, pointing to all-inclusive development efforts and active local participation in initiatives like the Bastar Olympics and the Bastar Pandum festival. Highlighting the nation's civilisational heritage, the President said that Sarnath, the site of Lord Buddha's first sermon, was included in the UNESCO World Heritage List this year, following the listing of 12 Maratha military forts last year. She stated that India proudly balances monuments of deep spirituality with historic symbols of military strength and resilience. Addressing foreign policy, she reiterated that peace, dialogue, cooperation, and the ideal of 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' (the world is one family) remain the bedrock of India's international relations. "We believe in a rules-based international order. Our endeavour is to ensure that the global community receives appropriate representation in the United Nations and other multilateral organisations," she stated, noting India's growing stature among Global South nations. The President also touched upon senior care, pointing out that alongside the world's largest young population, India is also seeing a rise in senior citizens and noted that about six crore senior citizens aged 70 and above can now avail of free healthcare services up to Rs 5 lakh per year under government initiatives, urging society to remain sensitive and uphold their dignity. She said the country is moving steadily towards building a 'Viksit Bharat' by 2047, driven by economic resilience, massive digital infrastructure, and empowered youth and women. She stressed that guided by the spirit of 'Antyodaya', the core resolve of the nation remains ensuring the fruits of development reach every individual, even as global warfare and instability present severe economic headwinds worldwide. "Even in such trying circumstances, our economy is moving ahead as the fastest growing major economy in the world. According to economic projections, the growth rate of the Indian economy is expected to be more than twice the average global growth rate. "'Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan' has further strengthened the foundation of our economic progress and national security," she said. Highlighting internal welfare milestones over the past decade, the President said that more than 25 crore people have been lifted out of poverty and added that nearly 59 crore account holders have joined the banking system under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, with over 32 crore of these account holders being women, while food security has been ensured for over 80 crore people through free rations. Underlining India's technological leap, she pointed out that the country has developed the world's largest and best digital infrastructure, accounting for more than half of global real-time digital transactions. Highlighting the demographic dividend, the President said that 65 per cent of the country's population is below the age of 35, describing the youth as India's "most valuable asset." She commended young entrepreneurs for driving a robust startup ecosystem and lauded young innovators, citing a recent space exploration milestone led by a team with an average age of just 28 years. Women's empowerment remained a central theme of her address. Celebrating achievements ranging from rural self-help groups to high-altitude defence, she said that the initial target of creating three crore 'Lakhpati Didis' has been achieved, with the government now pushing towards a goal of creating three crore more. "Our girls are performing exceptionally well in education and diverse sectors, from the Drone Didi enhancing agricultural productivity to the Fighter Combat Leader in the Air Force. In the recently concluded Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, women won 8 out of India's total tally of 13 gold medals," she said. The President also highlighted political inclusion, pointing out that the enactment of the 'Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam' in 2023, which reserves 33 per cent of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and Legislative Assemblies, will make Indian democracy more inclusive. Speaking on sustainable development, she asserted that India is playing a leading role globally in protecting the environment, having achieved several Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for 2030 ahead of schedule. Reciting a Santali language poem penned by Pandit Raghunath Murmu, she urged citizens to remain committed to preserving nature and human values, linking individual action to national initiatives such as 'Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam' and 'Lifestyle for Environment' (LiFE). The President also paid homage to freedom fighters, Mahatma Gandhi, B R Ambedkar and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel for integrating over 550 princely states. She also solemnly remembered those who lost their lives or faced displacement during partition, observed on August 14 as 'Vibhajan Vibheeshika Smriti Divas'. She invoked Telugu writer Gurajada Apparao's lines, "A nation is not just its land, a nation is all its people", urging every citizen to contribute wholeheartedly to transforming independent India into a fully developed nation by 2047.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday (August 14, 2026) quashed criminal proceedings against YouTuber and comedian Samay Raina and four others for their remarks about people with disabilities on the show, India’s Got Latent.
A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant also quashed the FIRs against Vipul Goyal, Balraj Paramjeet Singh Ghai, Sonali Thakkar and Nishant Jagdish Tanwar.

The top court appreciated the efforts made by them in organising a chess tournament in March for specially abled persons and helping raise awareness about organisations working for persons with disabilities, including the ones supporting those suffering from rare diseases such as Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA).
“Once there are genuine efforts, positive results are bound to be there… They are very bright youngsters.
If they start working in the positive direction, they will bring positive results,” Chief Justice Kant said.
The top court was hearing pleas, including the one filed by M/s SMA Cure Foundation, which works for individuals affected by rare SMA disease.

During the hearing, senior advocate Aparajita Singh, appearing for the foundation, said that pursuant to the apex court’s order, Mr. Raina and the others had made “genuine efforts” to engage with the foundation.
“This matter was going nowhere till this court took a very strong stand last time,” Ms. Singh said.
While quashing the FIR and related proceedings against them, the Bench said the matter concerning these five influencers stood closed.
During the hearing, the Chief Justice said that he and other Supreme Court judges had the opportunity to interact with a delegation of persons with disabilities on Thursday (August 13, 2026).
“It was quite a learning experience and an eye-opener for us to meet them,” the Chief Justice said.

article_sentences: Union Minister for Coal and Mines G. Kishan Reddy on Friday alleged that ‘certain malicious elements’ were conspiring to ‘incite attacks’ on Parliament and the Supreme Court, hoping to create a situation in India similar to the political turmoil witnessed in countries such as Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal.

He further claimed that ‘some Opposition forces’ within the country were ‘distressed’ by India’s progress, much like Pakistan and Bangladesh, which, he said, viewed India’s development with envy and anxiety at the National Tricolour Rally (Tiranga Yatra) organised by the Telangana BJP from the Dr. B.R. Ambedkar statue at Tank Bund to the Swami Vivekananda statue on the eve of Independence Day.

The Union Minister alleged that people were aware of how certain political parties and what he termed ‘Tukde-Tukde gangs’ had behaved during the events surrounding Operation Sindoor, claiming that they appeared to ‘want Pakistan to succeed and India to fail’.
“The people of the nation must reject the malicious politics of those who carry the Constitution in hand while engaging in anti-national conspiracies,” he said.
Calling for unity, Mr. Kishan Reddy said the need of the hour was for citizens to work together for the nation’s progress under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
He also challenged Chief Minister.
A. Revanth Reddy to take action against the AIMIM for allegedly opposing the singing of Vande Mataram.

Union Minister of State for Home Affairs Bandi Sanjay Kumar said the Congress should demonstrate its commitment to youth empowerment by providing opportunities to members of Generation Z in the State Cabinet.
Stating that there was broad agreement on the proposal to permit entry into legislative bodies at the age of 21, he called for a nationwide discussion on the issue.
Mr. Sanjay Kumar also urged the Congress to field Gen Z candidates in the forthcoming MLC elections and give greater representation to younger leaders while allotting Assembly tickets.
Telangana BJP president N. Ramchander Rao extended Independence Day greetings to the people of the State and thanked participants for joining the Tiranga Yatra with enthusiasm and discipline.
Rajya Sabha member and BJP OBC Morcha national president K. Laxman said India’s strength lay in its unity despite its linguistic, religious, regional and cultural diversity.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday (August 14) imposed a cost of Rs.
for prolonging a 20-year-old commercial suit filed by NTPC.
The cost imposed was directed to be deposited with the Supreme Court Advocates on Record Association.

A bench of Justice PS Narasimha and Justice Alok Aradhe strongly disapproved of RIL's litigation strategy, noting that the suit filed in 2005 is still at the evidence stage, with the company raising objections at every turn.
“The following facts would reveal that the power of the RIL to litigate and obstruct progress of the suit seems unlimited.

There is no dearth of financial resources, no obligation to aid and assist the court to cope with pending backlog of cases, perhaps it is lucrative for RIL to raise some objection or the other at every stage and when the trial court rejects it, the appellate and special leave jurisdictions open up…it is compelling for us to note that the suit filed by NTPC way back in 2005 has not progressed much.
At every stage there has been obstruction… In all, two decades have passed by and the suit is still at the stage of evidence.”, the Court observed.
The dispute arises out of a 2005 suit filed by NTPC against Reliance Industries Ltd.
(RIL) seeking specific performance of a natural gas supply agreement.
Despite being pending for more than 20 years, the suit has not proceeded beyond the evidence stage.
During the course of the proceedings, RIL filed a series of applications and appeals challenging various procedural orders.

First, it sought discovery of NTPC's internal documents, but the application was rejected by both the Single Judge and the Division Bench as a belated "fishing enquiry." RIL subsequently attempted to introduce its own internal documents on record, but that request was also rejected, and its challenge before the Supreme Court was later withdrawn.
